data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A small research team should adopt an existing experiment tracker and wrap it with a lightweight, custom 'orchestration layer' only if active learning loops are required; otherwise, the integration tax of building a full tracker outweighs the benefits, provided the existing tool supports event-driven hooks to avoid the migration cliff.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If no existing tool supports the specific low-latency event stream required for the active learning loop.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the team's definition of 'experiment' evolves to require complex state machine transitions not supported by standard trackers.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'orchestration layer' becomes so complex that it effectively duplicates the functionality of a custom tracker, negating the time savings.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The decision hinges on the 'Control Coupling Coefficient': if the experiment requires the tracker to synchronously modify parameters (high coupling), a custom build or deep fork is necessary to maintain causal integrity. If the interaction is asynchronous (low coupling), existing tools with webhook capabilities suffice. This avoids the 'integration tax' by limiting custom code to the orchestration logic rather than data storage, while preventing the 'migration cliff' by enforcing a strict schema via the wrapper from day one.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
